Article Title: Asian Games: Manu Bhaker returns empty-handed after four medal events as India’s shooting campaign falls short of Hangzhou
Article Text:
Manu Bhaker (PTI Photo)

Manu’s four-event campaign ends without a podium

ALSO READ:

Shooting still one of India’s biggest medal contributor, but gold returns lag

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will return from the Asian Games 2026 without a medal after competing in four events in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan — an unexpected outcome for one of India’s biggest medal hopes and another indication of the shooting contingent’s struggles to match its record haul from the previous edition.India had won 22 shooting medals, including seven gold, at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. In Aichi-Nagoya, the Indian shooters have so far managed 12 medals, with only one gold, with just five trap medal events remaining in the competition. Esha Singh’s silver in the women’s 25m pistol on Monday added to the tally, but the overall campaign has lacked the gold-medal returns India had hoped for.Manu entered the Games as one of India’s biggest medal contenders after her historic double bronze at the Paris Olympics and strong recent international form. But the 24-year-old could not convert her four medal opportunities into a podium finish.Her campaign began with the women’s 10m air pistol events. Manu qualified third for the individual final with 579 points but finished fifth after scoring 181.1 in the medal round. India also narrowly missed a medal in the corresponding team event, finishing fourth.The 25m pistol events offered another opportunity, but Manu missed the individual final after scoring 579-18x in qualification to finish 11th.She then ended her campaign on Monday as India finished fifth in the 25m pistol team event.The Indian trio of Esha Singh, Manu and Rahi Sarnobat scored 1727-56x. China won gold with 1743-68x, South Korea took silver with 1735-65x and Chinese Taipei claimed bronze with 1734-48x.Esha provided a bright spot by winning silver in the individual 25m pistol final after an exhausting series of shoot-offs, giving India another shooting medal.Despite Manu’s disappointment, shooting remains one of India’s most productive disciplines at Aichi-Nagoya. The contingent has delivered 12 medals so far, but the haul includes only one gold, a sharp contrast to the seven gold medals and 22 total shooting medals India collected at Hangzhou.Manu had arrived in Japan in good form. She won bronze at the 2026 ISSF World Cup in Hangzhou, while Esha claimed gold in the women’s 25m pistol at the same event. At the ISSF World Cup in Munich, Manu also won silver in the 10m air pistol mixed team event with Samrat Rana. She subsequently won individual silver in the women’s 25m pistol at the Asian Shooting Championships.Her father, Ram Kishan Bhaker, acknowledged that her performance had fallen below the standards she had established.“Manu's performance was not as per her standard because she set a very high standard and expectation for the Indian fans. As per my expectations, her score must be more than 585; it should be more than 585 to 595. Today's score was not enough...” he told IANS.He also questioned the circumstances surrounding Rahi Sarnobat’s crucial miss in the 25m pistol qualification.“Rahi was shooting very well, but suddenly one shot was not showing, which I believe may be the technical glitch or something else.”“But, later on the jury said that the shot went out of target, which certainly I don't believe, because Rahi is a very experienced shooter, and it could be something else. Let the jury test what it is or otherwise everything was going well,” he added.With five trap medal events still to come, India can add to its shooting tally. But with the likes of Manu unable to convert multiple medal opportunities, the discipline’s overall performance in Aichi-Nagoya has so far fallen well short of the extraordinary returns from Hangzhou.
Article Summary: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will return from the Asian Games 2026 without a medal after competing in four events. The 24-year-old could not convert her four medal opportunities into a podium finish. India had won 22 shooting medals, including seven gold, at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023.

Article Title: Asian Games: How a rare, inexplicable miss by Rahi Sarnobat cost India a 25m pistol team medal
Article Text:
India's Rahi Sarnobat competes during the rapid stage of the women's 25m pistol qualification event. (PTI Photo)

How one miss changed India’s medal prospects

Esha Singh salvages an individual silver

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India were left ruing a costly and extraordinary lapse by experienced shooter Rahi Sarnobat after a rare miss in the women’s 25m pistol team event derailed their medal hopes at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Monday. Sarnobat’s shot yielded zero points in the fourth series, a setback that proved decisive as India finished fifth, outside the medal positions.The Indian trio of Esha Singh Manu Bhaker and Sarnobat combined for a score of 1727-56x in the team competition. China won gold with 1743-68x, while South Korea (1735-65x) and Chinese Taipei (1734-48x) took silver and bronze, respectively.For Sarnobat, a former Asian Games gold medallist, the incident was particularly difficult to explain. The shooter herself admitted that she had never experienced anything similar in her career."This is the first time that something like this has happened in my career and I do not know how it happened," Sarnobat said.Her unexpected zero in a competition where every shot counts left India with little room to recover and turned what could have been a medal-winning performance into a disappointing fifth-place finish.The women’s 25m pistol event featured both team and individual competitions, with India fielding three experienced shooters in Esha, Manu and Sarnobat. While Esha kept India’s hopes alive in the individual event, the team’s medal ambitions took a major hit during the qualification rounds.Sarnobat endured a difficult fourth series, registering a score of just 39. The series consisted of five shots, and her performance included the rare miss that resulted in zero points. The setback was particularly damaging in a tightly contested competition, where the margin separating the medal-winning teams was relatively small.Sarnobat eventually finished 30th in the individual qualification standings with a score of 568-16x. Her teammates also had contrasting fortunes in the individual event. Esha qualified for the final in eighth place with 580-22x, while Manu narrowly missed out, finishing 11th with 579-18x.India’s final team score of 1727-56x left them 7 points behind bronze medallists Chinese Taipei and just 8 points behind silver medallists South Korea. The gap to the gold-winning Chinese team was 16 points, underlining the impact of the team’s missed opportunities.Sarnobat, who won gold in the women’s 25m pistol at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, was among India’s most experienced competitors in the discipline. Her admission that she could not explain the unusual mistake added to the disappointment of a campaign in which India had entered the event with medal aspirations.While India missed out on a team medal, Esha produced a determined performance in the individual event to secure silver after an exceptionally long final.The 21-year-old from Hyderabad, the reigning world number one, fought through five shoot-offs, including three to move into medal contention and two more in the gold-medal contest against China’s Xiao Jiaruixuan.Both shooters finished regulation with scores of 38, forcing another shoot-off to decide the winner. Esha faltered on the final shot, allowing Xiao to take gold by a single shot. North Korea’s Kim Hyon Suk claimed bronze after losing her shoot-off against Esha, finishing with 34 points."Yes, I was under pressure and this is the longest match of my career so far. My arms were aching at the end of it," Esha said after the final.For Manu, meanwhile, the Asian Games ended without an individual medal. The two-time Olympic medallist had already finished fifth in the women’s 10m air pistol event and was unable to qualify for the 25m pistol final.
Article Summary: India finish fifth in women's 25m pistol team event at Asian Games 2026. Rahi Sarnobat's shot yielded zero points in the fourth series, a setback that proved decisive. China won gold with 1743-68x, while South Korea and Chinese Taipei took silver and bronze.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: India’s 44-year wait ends as Sawan Barwal wins silver in men’s marathon
Article Text:
India's Sawan Barwal reacts after his second place finish in the men's marathon at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Lee Jin-man)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Historic medal for Indian athletics

Sawan Barwal scripted history at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday, winning silver in the men’s marathon and ending India’s 44-year wait for a medal in the event. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing 48 seconds behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita, who won gold in 2:10:49. China’s Peiyou Feng took bronze with 2:12:13.The marathon started at 4 a.m. IST with 19 runners, including Barwal and fellow Indian Kartik Karkera. Barwal quickly established himself among the leaders and was in second place at the halfway mark with a timing of 1:05:54. He continued to hold his position as the race entered its final stages, reaching the 35-kilometre mark in second.With around seven kilometres left, Barwal was still chasing Yamashita. The Japanese runner eventually opened up a gap, but Barwal maintained his pace and stayed firmly in silver-medal position. He finished with a timing of 2:11:37, securing India’s first Asian Games marathon medal since the 1982 Delhi Games and the country’s first medal in the event on foreign soil.The silver adds to Barwal’s growing record. In April, he broke Shivnath Singh’s 48-year-old national marathon record at the NN Marathon Rotterdam.His latest performance now converts that record-setting form into a major international medal.Barwal’s silver is India’s fourth Asian Games marathon medal. Chhota Singh won gold and Surat Singh Mathur took bronze at the inaugural 1951 Games, while Hosur Kukkappa Seetharan won another bronze in 1982.The other Indian runner, Kartik Karkera, finished 17th among 19 competitors with a time of 2:22:41.
Article Summary: Sawan Barwal won silver in the men's marathon at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing 48 seconds behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita, who won gold in 2:10:49. It is India's first Asian Games marathon medal since the 1982 Delhi Games.

Article Title: 'Not too much pressure': How Zhu Jiner turned struggles in India into taking China closer to Chess Olympiad gold | Exclusive
Article Text:
China's Zhu Jiner at Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

Finding warmth amid a difficult campaign

From four-year-old beginner to China’s Board 1

Steering the ship in Samarkand

ALSO READ:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(Indian women's team takes on China in the penultimate round of Chess Olympiad on Saturday.)

NEW DELHI: The 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad is currently edging towards its climax in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. In the women's section, one team has pulled clear of the rest, and it is China, the comfortable leaders at the moment. And if anything doesn't go south, it will be the Chinese girls donning the gold medals around their necks at the end of 11 rounds of play. But do you know the most interesting thing in it? China don't even have their strongest players in the event.As per the current FIDE ratings, none of the world top three, which include Hou Yifan, the current women's world champion Ju Wenjun, and Lei Tingjie, is part of this Chinese side. Zhu Jiner, the world no. 4, is thus on Board 1, facing the toughest of the top board opponents at this Samarkand Olympiad. And she has risen to the challenge, remaining unbeaten throughout, a complete turnaround from her form at the Global Chess League (GCL) in India just a couple of weeks earlier.Just before the Olympiad, Jiner was part of the two-time GCL champion Triveni Continental Kings, who had a torrid event as they finished second from bottom in the group stage this time.Jiner's performance was not up to the mark either, with the 23-year-old Grandmaster winning just one, losing four and drawing five games in the tournament.The on-board results, coupled with the hectic schedule, meant little time or urge for her to enjoy the city of Bengaluru, the host of this fourth edition of GCL.Despite her struggles on the board, Jiner maintained a deep appreciation for the host nation. "This is my first time in Bengaluru, and overall, I’ve had a very good impression of the city. The weather is also very pleasant," Jiner told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction."Since I’m here mainly to compete in the Global Chess League, there’s been quite a lot of time spent on matches and preparation, so I haven’t really had much time to go out. When I have a game, most of my energy is focused on the competition."Bengaluru was simply the latest stop in Jiner’s long-standing relationship with Indian chess venues, having previously played across the country's major hubs."I’ve been to India several times before. I’ve visited New Delhi, Pune, Mumbai, and now Bengaluru, all for international chess tournaments," she recounted. "What I like most about India is how passionate people are about chess. Whether they’re players or fans, you can really feel their love for the game. For example, during this Global Chess League, the players have received such a warm welcome from the local fans. Every day, when we come out of the playing venue, there are so many chess fans waiting to get autographs or take photos with their idols. That atmosphere has left a very deep impression on me."Jiner also noted the broader cultural and competitive ties between the two Asian superpowers, acknowledging the explosive growth of Indian chess talent on the global stage."I think India has a very long and rich history and culture. I’ve heard some Indian mythological stories as well," she observed. "At the same time, India is a very vibrant and rapidly developing country, and there is a lot of trade and exchange between the two countries (India and China). As far as modern chess is concerned, India has developed incredibly quickly over the past few years, especially when it comes to the younger generation. There are now many very talented young Indian players, and they have achieved excellent results in international competitions again and again."Jiner's journey to leading China's national team on Board 1 in Samarkand was built on decades of steady progression. "I was introduced to chess when I was about four years old. At first, it was very simple, I just thought the game was interesting and enjoyed playing it," Jiner recalled."Then, when I was around seven, I joined the Zhejiang team and began receiving more systematic training. Later, I joined the national team and gradually started competing at higher and higher levels. Actually, there wasn’t one particular moment when I suddenly decided, 'I want to become a professional chess player.' It happened gradually. Over time, chess became a very important part of my life, and eventually becoming a professional player felt like a natural choice for me. "Her personal trajectory mirrors the unique structure of Chinese chess. "Chess came to China relatively late. It has been around for many years now, but compared with some other sports, it is still a relatively niche sport," Jiner explained."I’m not very familiar with the current development system for young Chinese players, but I think for a little girl who is just starting to learn chess, the most important thing is to first develop a genuine love for the game. The professional path is actually very long, and there will be many difficulties along the way. If you really love the sport, that’s what will help you keep going."That resilience proved essential as China arrived in Samarkand without its standard contingent of World Champions. Leading an understrength team, Jiner reframed the narrative, turning the absence of superstars into a source of resolve."I think China has some of the strongest female players in the world, and overall, the team has consistently been among the strongest," Jiner noted before the start of the tournament. "However, this time, the Chinese team hasn’t been able to compete at the Olympiad with its most complete and strongest lineup, which I personally feel is a little unfortunate."Rather than letting the pressure of top-board responsibility overwhelm her squad after the setback in India, Jiner embraced the lowered expectations, which has worked well for her and her team so far."Of course, even under these circumstances, the Chinese women's team is still a very strong team. But there are many strong teams at this Olympiad, and I think the competition between them will be extremely intense. So I wouldn’t consider China the biggest favourite to win the title.For us, that actually means there isn’t too much pressure. We’ll prepare carefully for each round, focus on the opponent in front of us, try to play at our best, and aim for a good result. "Jiner may not have considered China the biggest favourite to win the title. But that pragmatic, round-by-round focus is now on the verge of delivering one of the most remarkable gold medal runs in modern Olympiad history.
Article Summary: World no. 4 Zhu Jiner is leading China's women's team at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. The 23-year-old Grandmaster is unbeaten on Board 1, a complete turnaround from her form at the Global Chess League (GCL) in India just a couple of weeks earlier.

Article Title: Week after losing coach, grieving Diya Chitale gets a moment to savour at Asian Games
Article Text:
Manush Shah and Diya Chitale (File photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Diya Chitale, the last seven days have been an emotional roller coaster. Exactly a week after losing Peter Engel, her coach since 2015, Diya stood on the Asian Games podium in Nagoya with the bronze medal around her neck, alongside Manush Shah. The duo had their moments against China’s top pairing of Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha before going down (0-4) 8-11, 5-11, 8-11, 2-11 in the mixed doubles semifinals at Sky Hall Toyota in Nagoya, settling for bronze. Despite the loss, Diya and Shah secured India’s first table-tennis medal of the ongoing Games.For Diya, Engel — who died on Sept 18 at 72 — was far more than a coach. “I had been working with Engel sir since 2015 and he is the person who completely developed my game. He was my go-to person for everything in TT,” she told TOI from Nagoya. Apart from the personal tragedy, there was also a lean spell for Diya and Shah to overcome. The world No. 8 mixed doubles pair had won two titles and finished runners-up once early in 2026, but their results dipped from June onwards. “I always believed that we are among the top few pairs and we can beat any pair on our day,” she said. Their belief was tested earlier on Friday.Drawn against Hong Kong’s world No. 4 Doo Hoi Kem and Wong Chun Ting, a pair they had lost to three times, the Indians knew execution had to be precise. They delivered, winning 3-1 (11-6, 13-15, 11-9, 11-5) to assure the nation its first TT medal of the Games before losing in semifinals. “We had played against them thrice and lost all our matches, but the last two matches were pretty close,” Diya said. “Hence we knew that if we had a clear strategy and if we could execute that well, we had a good chance.And we were able to do that today.”The medal carries weight far beyond the colour. It is India’s second Asian Games mixed doubles medal, after Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra’s bronze in Jakarta in 2018. “Winning a medal at the Games in our sport is huge and extra sweet since all the powerhouses in TT come from Asia — China, Japan, South Korea and so on,” she said. Diya dedicated her medal to Engel, paying her a personal tribute. “It would have been wonderful for him to see me achieve this today. This medal is for him.”
Article Summary: Diya Chitale and Manush Shah secure India's first table-tennis medal of the Games. They beat Hong Kong's world No. 4 Doo Hoi Kem and Wong Chun Ting 3-1. But they lost in semifinals to China's top pairing of Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha.

Article Title: D Gukesh ‘tricks’ Germany, keeps Indian challenge alive at Chess Olympiad
Article Text:
D Gukesh (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany in the ninth round of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand on Friday.The win helped India move to 15 match-points, one behind leaders and hosts Uzbekistan (16), who humbled USA. Nodirbek Yakubboev scored another crucial win for the hosts, this time over Hans Niemann. Uzbekistan’s second-strength team and Armenia are also level with India on points with just two rounds remaining.India women (15 points) humbled Uzbekistan 3-1 but are still trailing China (17) by two match-points. China, who have not fielded their full-strength team, continued their march towards the gold medal with a win over Armenia, in which Zhu Jiner and Lu Miaoyi scored full points.The draw between Kazakhstan and Mongolia (15 each) also helped India, as neither could overtake them. Divya Deshmukh and Vanitka Agrawal, individual gold medallists in the last Olympiad, scripted the success of the Indian women as they defeated lower-rated opponents.B Savitha Shri’s stunning sequence of seven successive wins came to an end with a draw against Guildona Karimova (Elo 2242), while K Humpy held her own on the top board.World champion Gukesh once again showed why he is such a dangerous rival. Germany, somewhat surprisingly, decided to rest Rasmus Svane, who had two successive wins in the preceding rounds, and chose to field Donchenko against Gukesh.The 28-year-old German almost justified the faith shown in him by pushing Gukesh to a corner. However, he then gave too much importance to Gukesh’s h-pawn and misplaced his pieces.ALSO READ: 'Not too much pressure': How Zhu Jiner turned struggles in India into taking China closer to Chess Olympiad gold | Exclusive While this drama was unfolding, Nihal Sarin had already drawn his game against Frederik Svane despite flirting with danger and mental abyss. R Praggnanandhaa and Erigaisi Arjun were unable to break through the defences of Vincent Keymer and Matthias Blubaum respectively.Arjun had even sacrificed his knight but reached a queen-and-extra-pawns versus queen, bishop-and-pawns endgame. However, with Gukesh turning the tables, the draws by Arjun and Praggnanandhaa were no longer a losing cause.
Article Summary: Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany. The win helped India move to 15 match-points, one behind leaders and hosts Uzbekistan (16), who humbled USA. Uzbekistan’s second-strength team and Armenia are also level with India on points with just two rounds remaining.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Joshna Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar settle for bronze in Squash mixed doubles
Article Text:
India's Joshana Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar settle for bronze. (PTI Photo)

India lose first game by narrowest margin

Joshna, Velavan hit back in style

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar came agonisingly close to a place in the Asian Games mixed doubles final, losing a dramatic semifinal to Hong Kong’s Tang Ming Hong and Lee Ka Yi 1-2 (10-11, 11-2, 11-10).The Indian pair looked to have one foot in the final after fighting back from a tight opening-game defeat and dominating the second. They then led 9-7 in the decider and had three match points, only for the Hong Kong pair to stage a stunning comeback and snatch the contest in a nerve-wracking finish.The defeat meant Joshna and Velavan had to settle for a bronze medal.The opening game was a tense battle with neither pair able to establish a significant advantage. Joshna and Velavan edged ahead at one stage, but Tang and Lee responded with three straight points to move 9-8 ahead. The Indians quickly levelled at 9-9 before Hong Kong earned game point.India fought back again to make it 10-10, but Tang and Lee won the next point to take the game 11-10 and move within one game of the final.The Indians responded emphatically in the second game. Joshna and Velavan came out aggressively, looking to finish points quickly rather than getting drawn into the long rallies that had characterised the opening game.They raced into a 3-0 lead and extended it to 7-2. From there, they did not give Hong Kong another point, closing out the game 11-2 to force a decider. Three match points slip away in dramatic deciderThe deciding game produced the most intense action of the contest. Joshna and Velavan initially trailed 2-5 but fought back to make it 4-5. The game then turned into a battle of attrition, with long rallies and several 'lets', where a point is replayed because of an obstruction, adding to the tension.The Indians eventually levelled at 6-6 before taking control. They moved 8-7 ahead and then stretched their lead to 9-7, with Velavan producing some outstanding defensive work. At 9-7, India had three match points but could not convert them. Tang and Lee held their nerve to win the next three points and level the game at 10-10.The next rally was fiercely contested and ended in controversy. India initially appeared to have won the point, with Velavan briefly celebrating, but the point was disallowed. Hong Kong then won the following point to complete a remarkable 11-10 comeback and book their place in the final.

Article Title: Khalid Jamil's India hold Panama to memorable 1-1 draw
Article Text:
India's Ryan Williams, right, shoots at goal as Panama's Roderick Miller defends during an international friendly soccer match between India and Panama in Bengaluru, India, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

It was an unforgettable Friday for the Indian football fans as the Blue Tigers fought on level terms with World Cup participants Panama, forcing a 1-1 draw from their famous visitors at Sree Kanteerava Stadium here.Panama, who played against Ghana, Croatia and England at the World Cup, had to dig deep as they rallied to avoid defeat against 138-ranked India in the FIFA international friendly.The hosts took the lead against the run of play, against a team 94 places above them in the world rankings, thanks to a clinical finish by striker Ryan Williams in the 41st minute. The visitors, who started with just three World Cuppers, made changes at the start of second half and the complexion of the game soon changed.Panama found the equaliser in the 67th minute after the entry of Azarias Londono, Jiovani Ramos and Omar Valencia in the second half. Valencia, the defender who plays for the New York Red Bulls in Major League Soccer, fired Panama’s equaliser with a long-range stunner.It was a well worked goal as Londono relayed the ball to defender Eduardo Gomez who found Valencia with a clear view of the goal. India wasted a golden chance in the 79th minute but Edmund Lalrindika failed to apply finishing touches to a perfectly-weighted pass from Ashique Kuruniyan.Sedate first half: Panama coach Thomas Christiansen was enjoying the cool Bengaluru weather, following a brief spell of rain which took the temperature to 22 degrees Celsius, watching his team press against a dogged Indian defence before his team went behind. The smile on his face vanished as he walked to the dressing room when the referee blew the half-time whistle as Williams put India ahead four minutes before the break.Until then, the visitors held the upper hand with more possession (58 per cent) and more shots (6), two of which were on target. However, the Indian team ensured they gave their famous rivals a good fight. It was a superb result for India coach Khalid Jamil who will now look forward to the same spirited show against former world champions Uruguay and Brazil.
Article Summary: India drew 1-1 with Panama at Sree Kanteerava Stadium in Bengaluru. Ryan Williams opened the scoring for the hosts in the 41st minute. Omar Valencia equalised in the 67th minute with a long-range stunner.

Article Title: Shock exit for Satwik-Chirag as Asian Games title defence ends in first round
Article Text:
Asian Games 2026: Thailand's Sukphun-Pakkapon stun defending champions Satwik-Chirag in R32

Tanisha-Dhruv advance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Defending champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty suffered a major setback at the Asian Games, crashing out in the first round after losing to Thailand’s Pakkapon Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun on Friday.The Indian pair started strongly, winning the opening game 21-12, but failed to maintain their momentum. The world No. 36 Thai duo fought back to win the next two games 21-19, 21-14 in 64 minutes.Satwik and Chirag looked set for a routine victory after dominating the first game, but the Thais made the most of the Indians’ errors in the second. With the score at 18-19, Satwik’s return went into the net to give Thailand a game point. The Indians saved one, but Pakkapon produced a superb cross-court winner to level the match.The deciding game turned one-sided as Satwik and Chirag appeared increasingly fatigued. Their returns lacked their usual power, forcing the world’s best attacking pair into an unfamiliar defensive role as the Thais repeatedly unleashed smashes.The defeat came after a demanding schedule and limited recovery time. Satwik said the team had returned late from the previous night’s event.“Quite patchy... We know these situations will happen. It will get tense because it will be tricky playing continuously in the team event. We were here till 12 last night,” Satwik told reporters.He also admitted that the pair needed to improve their mental approach.“It’s the mental part. Whenever we are mentally free, I think no one can beat us. But when we are stuck anywhere, we give opponents a chance to beat us,” he said.There was better news for India in mixed doubles, with Tanisha Crasto and Dhruv Kapila reaching the quarterfinals after two contrasting wins.They began with a comfortable 21-8, 21-7 victory over Maldives’ Nibal Ahmed and Aminath Nabeeha Abdul Razzaq in just 21 minutes. They were then pushed hard by Malaysia’s Shevon Jemie Lai and Soon Huat Goh but held their nerve to win 22-20, 24-22 in an hour.Tanisha and Dhruv will face China’s Yan Zhe Feng and Dongping Huang in the quarterfinals.World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand and Unnati Hooda also won their opening-round matches. Hooda defeated North Korea’s Mi Song Yu 21-9, 21-10 in 30 minutes.India’s second men’s doubles pair, Hariharan Amsakarunan and MR Arjun, however, lost 14-21, 11-21 to second-seeded Indonesians Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohi
Article Summary: Defending champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty lose to Thailand's Pakkapon Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun. World No. 36 Thai duo fought back to win the next two games 21-19, 21-14 in 64 minutes. Tanisha Crasto and Dhruv Kapila reach the quarterfinals after two contrasting wins.

Article Title: DDCA joint secretary raises concerns over Delhi selector, support staff appointments
Article Text:
A view of the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi. (PTI Photo/Kamal Kishore)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) joint secretary Amit Grover has formally raised reservations over the proposed appointments of Varun Sood and Manu Nayyar as part of the Delhi cricket setup, questioning whether they meet the prescribed eligibility criteria.In an email sent to members of the Cricket Advisory Committee (CAC) on Friday, a copy of which TimesofIndia.com has, Grover said he wanted to place his concerns on record before the selection process concluded. He urged the committee to examine the relevant records and applicable rules before making any final decision on the proposed appointments. The email is addressed to members of the CAC and copied to the DDCA top brass.“With regard to the proposed appointments of coaches and selectors, I wish to formally place on record my reservations concerning the proposed appointment of Mr. Varun Sood and Mr. Manu Nayyar, particularly with regard to their eligibility and compliance with the prescribed criteria,” Grover wrote in the email.Manu Nayyar has been appointed as selector for the senior men’s team and Varun Sood as assistant coach for the men’s U-19 team.It is worth noting that there was an issue with Nayyar's availability last season as he was reportedly missing due to committments in an overseas league, when the teams were being picked at DDCA.“All the rules have been followed diligently. Everyone who has been appointed has played cricket at the highest level. They have been in the system for a long time. Manu Nayyar is yet to complete his five-year term, whereas Varun has recently retired from playing cricket and knows a thing or two about how modern-day cricket functions. We are all thinking about the betterment of Delhi cricket, and these accusations are needless,” said a recipient of the email.TimesofIndia.com reached out to DDCA secretary Ashok Sharma for a comment but received no response.Former India wicketkeeper Vijay Dahiya has been reappointed as head coach of the Delhi Ranji Trophy team as the DDCA named coaches, mentors and High Performance Centre staff, with several former players and their sons also finding assignments in the appointments. There are 22 coaches, including head coaches, assistant coaches, bowling coaches and fielding coaches, appointed across the senior men’s team to the U-14 level, while 18 have been appointed across various women’s teams.Meanwhile, Grover emphasised that the concerns had been communicated before the completion of the selection process and, therefore, should be considered by the CAC before any appointment was finalised. He said the committee should satisfy itself that all eligibility conditions and prescribed criteria had been complied with.The DDCA joint secretary also questioned the proposed composition of the selection panel, pointing out that it appeared to substantially comprise the same selectors who were associated with the process last year.His concern comes against the backdrop of what he described as disappointing performances by Delhi cricket. Grover acknowledged that continuity could have its merits but urged the CAC to exercise “greater care and circumspection” while selecting coaches and selectors. He said recent performances, along with eligibility, experience and the overall requirements of Delhi cricket, should be taken into account when making the appointments.“I therefore request the CAC to independently examine all relevant records and applicable criteria before taking any final decision,” Grover wrote, while also requesting that his communication be treated as part of the official record of the selection and appointment process.
Article Summary: Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) joint secretary Amit Grover has formally raised reservations over the proposed appointments of Varun Sood and Manu Nayyar. Grover questioned whether they meet the prescribed eligibility criteria. He urged the committee to examine the relevant records and applicable rules before making any final decision.

India’s shooting tally reaches 10 medals

NEW DELHI: India’s shooters missed out on a medal in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions individual event at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday, despite securing silver in the team competition earlier in the day. Asian record holder Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists, bringing a disappointing end to India’s campaign in the event.Aishwary, who had qualified third for the final, managed 327.6 points to finish fifth. Niraj, who had entered the final in fourth place in qualification, could only score 299 points to finish eighth.China’s Liu Yukun claimed gold with 360.5 points, setting a new Asian Games record. His compatriot Zhang Changhong took silver with 360.2 points, while Kazakhstan’s Islam Satpayev secured bronze with 348.3 points.The result was a setback for India after both shooters had shown promise in the qualification round. Aishwary, the Asian record holder, had finished third, while Niraj secured the fourth qualifying spot. However, neither could maintain that position in the final as China swept the top two places.The individual event disappointment followed India’s silver-medal finish in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions team competition. Aishwary, Niraj and Rudrankksh Patil combined for a score of 1762-94x, finishing just behind China, who secured gold with 1766-95x. South Korea took bronze with 1751-87x.Aishwary scored 589-34x to finish third in the team qualification standings, while Niraj recorded 588-34x to place fourth. Rudrankksh, with 585-26x, finished ninth and missed out on a place in the individual final.India had won gold in the team event at the 2022 Asian Games but surrendered their title to China in Aichi-Nagoya.India’s shooting contingent has now collected 10 medals at the 2026 Asian Games, including one gold, five silver and four bronze medals. The only shooting gold so far came on Friday, when Suruchi and Kamaljeet won the 10m mixed air pistol event.The Indian pair defeated South Korea 484.6 to 478.0 in the final, with Iran taking bronze on 415.8 points. India’s winning score also broke the Asian record of 481.3, previously set by Uzbekistan at the Asian Shooting Championships in New Delhi earlier this year.India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19 on Friday, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals. The women’s cricket team had earlier secured India’s other gold, defeating Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final.The rifle team silver added to India’s medal haul, but the failure to convert two strong qualification performances into an individual podium finish left the shooters without another medal in the event.

Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists. India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals.

Article Title: Defending Champions India through to Asian Games semi-final as rain washes out quarter-final against Afghanistan

India’s men’s cricket team advanced to the semi-finals of the 2026 Asian Games without taking the field after persistent rain forced their quarter-final against Afghanistan to be abandoned in Nisshin, Japan.With dark clouds and steady rain keeping the covers firmly in place and conditions showing no signs of improving, the match was eventually called off without a ball being bowled, sending India through to the last four under the tournament’s knockout rules.India will now face the winner of the Sri Lanka-Nepal quarter-final in the semi-finals as they continue their bid to retain the gold medal they won at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.India entered the tournament with a strong squad featuring several established international names. Their campaign in the previous edition also ended with a weather-affected final, with India awarded the gold medal after their title clash against Afghanistan was washed out.The Indian women’s team has already successfully defended its Asian Games title in Aichi-Nagoya. Harmanpreet Kaur-led India defeated Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final to claim the gold medal.Earlier, Pakistan also advanced to the men’s semi-finals after their quarter-final against Hong Kong, China was abandoned due to rain. Article Title: Asian Games: Rain threatens Shreyas Iyer-led India’s title defence ahead of Afghanistan quarterfinal
Article Text:

Nisshin: Even if a single ball is not bowled, the Indian men’s cricket team will still retain the Asian Games gold they won in the previous edition on debut. Going by the weather here, the situation cannot be ruled out. The only constant for the Indian team from the time they landed in Tokyo a week ago has been rain. Apart from a couple of indoor net sessions, the players have probably held an umbrella more than a bat or a ball.They arrived in Nagoya with a steady drizzle on Saturday afternoon and their practice session on Sunday was halted midway due to rain again. With the venue being a makeshift cricket stadium, there were no indoor facilities for the team to turn to.But skipper Shreyas Iyer refused to dwell on the weather conditions. “There is rain, but we can’t use that as an excuse. Such hurdles will keep coming. Irrespective of the situation, we are mentally prepared (to play). We got a decent warm-up and a little practice (before the rain). We will try to adapt as soon as possible to the wicket.” In the quarterfinals on Monday, they face Afghanistan.At the Korogi Sports Park here, Afghanistan come into the contest on the back of a mixed campaign so far.While they had an easy outing against hosts Japan in their campaign opener, they were handed a five-wicket loss by Nepal on Friday.The results are the outcome of the fact that Afghanistan is fielding a second-string team in the tournament with skipper Darwish Rasooli and Abdollah Ahmadzai, the only players in the squad from the team which lost to India 0-3 in a bilateral series recently.A full-strength Indian team against a rookie Afghanistan side may seem like a contest of the uneven, but the Indian team will know better than taking the Afghans lightly, especially after their near-loss. In the five-over rain-truncated contest India managed 32/4 and then scrapped through with a two-run margin.“We can’t take any team in the Asian Games lightly because the wicket here cannot be set to a particular standard. It will be challenging and difficult for every team.”Iyer also cited the example of the recent match against Japan, a rain-truncated contest. It will be interesting to see if India will risk playing Jasprit Bumrah, who was rested for the match against Japan, given he is coming back from injury and the outfield may not be the best.While the stage is set for the title defence, one can only hope for th srain to stay away, especially for the scores of Indian fans, who are planning to travel from across Japan to root for the men in blue.

India captain Shubman Gill believes the best way to get the most out of Virat Kohli is to simply let the star batter be himself.Kohli smashed an unbeaten 139 off 88 balls as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the first ODI at the Greenfield International Stadium on Sunday. The 30-ball ton was, oddly, the least surprising part of what Abhishek Sharma did at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. It isn't even his fastest hundred. What's odd about the innings is what it says about the number sitting next to that extraordinary strike rate: his average.Somewhere in Abhishek Sharma's memory, though, there's a faster century still. It came two years ago, for Punjab against Meghalaya in a Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy fixture nobody outside domestic cricket was watching: 28 balls, no fanfare.So when he reached three figures in 30 deliveries against Afghanistan in New Delhi, becoming the fastest T20I centurion ever produced by a Full Member nation and only the third-fastest in the format's history overall, it wasn't a discovery. It was a confirmation, delivered on a bigger stage, of something the data had already been saying for a while.The ground has some history with him already. Eight years earlier, on the same square when it was still called Feroz Shah Kotla, a 17-year-old Sharma walked out at number six for Delhi Daredevils against Royal Challengers Bangalore and top-scored on IPL debut — an unbeaten 46 off 19 balls. It was the innings that first put his name into circulation.None of that is really the story, though. The story is what his average has been doing while all this has been going on.After 58 T20I innings, Abhishek averages 33.18 at a strike rate of 194.55. Among those who have batted at least 20 times in T20Is since Abhishek's debut in July 2024, nobody has struck as quickly as his 194.55 per 100 balls.Put that alongside the numbers of his closest opening peers and the combination starts to look strange. Phil Salt, across almost the same number of innings, averages 34.34 at 165.89: a fraction higher on average, nearly thirty runs per hundred balls slower. Finn Allen's numbers read 28.67 and 170.74; Travis Head's, 28.40 and 156.69. Multiply strike rate by average and divide by 100 and you get a rough figure for scoring speed without giving up the average: Abhishek comes out at 64.56, against 56.97 for Salt, 48.95 for Allen and 44.50 for Head.The gap isn't really about six-hitting or bravado. It's that T20 cricket generally punishes extreme aggression with a lower average, and in Abhishek's case, over more than fifty innings now, it hasn't.Look closer and the shape of his batting explains some of it. Of his 1,858 T20I runs, 1,484 (79.9%) have come in boundaries. In the Afghanistan innings that figure spiked to 94.44%, the highest boundary share recorded in any men's T20I century.He hits a six in T20Is every 7.58 balls, comfortably ahead of Allen (8.47), Salt (12.47) and Head (14.20). Zoom out to his whole T20 career, across formats, and he reached his hundredth six faster, by balls faced, than anyone the format has seen, edging West Indies' Evin Lewis. Among Indian batters with 50 or more T20 sixes, nobody has matched his rate of clearing the boundary. He's the best of the lot, streets ahead of Sanju Samson, Shivam Dube, Suryakumar Yadav and Yuvraj Singh , the mentor whose fastest-fifty record he's now threatened on at least three occasions.The clearest expression of the method is the powerplay. His strike rate in an innings' first ten balls, 176, is the joint-highest on record, level with Tim David: he isn't feeling out the pitch before he attacks. His boundary percentage inside the powerplay, 33.48% according to CricViz, is the best among batters with 500-plus T20I runs.This has happened before, too. India have breached 90 in a T20I powerplay four times, and Abhishek has been the one doing the damage on every occasion: 59 not out off 21 against England at the Wankhede last year, 51 not out off 14 against New Zealand in Guwahati this year, 51 off 19 in the World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where he reached fifty in 18 balls under the most pressure he's likely ever faced. His 76 not out off 22 balls is simply the largest number yet on that list. His opening stand with Samson, 142 off 59 balls, is now the fastest century opening partnership for India in T20Is by run rate, overtaking a stand between KL Rahul and Rohit Sharma from Indore in 2017.None of this comes free. Abhishek walked into this year's T20 World Cup and made three consecutive ducks, followed that with 15, 10 and 9, and salvaged the campaign with two match-defining fifties, one in a must-win Super Eight game against Zimbabwe, the other in the final. Eight innings, 141 runs, an average of 17.62. "As a batter, as a cricketer, sometimes [my form is] going to go up and down," he said afterwards, and there's little sense he sees the ducks as a separate problem from the sixes. They're the same bet, landing differently.And 2026 has underlined that cost. Abhishek has been dismissed for a duck 10 times in T20 cricket this calendar year, the most by any batter in a year, ahead of Rashid Khan's nine in 2019 and Shadab Khan's nine in 2024. Five of those have come off the first ball, making him the joint-most prolific first-ball duck-maker in a calendar year in T20Is, alongside Rwanda's Kevin Irakoze in 2023 and Richard Ngarava in 2024.What's changed isn't the risk-taking. It's how deliberately he manages it. Against the Rashid Khan, Mohammad Nabi and Mujeeb Ur Rahman spin trio in the Afghanistan series, he made a conscious tactical switch, going only forward or down the pitch, never back, and scored 54 off 15 against them, including 4, 4, 6 off three straight Rashid deliveries in the last over of the powerplay.In the first two games, camped on the back foot against the same bowlers, he'd managed only 29 off 17. "It's always about me backing my shots because I don't have a lot of shots," he said earlier this year, after an 85 off 34 against New Zealand, which sounds like modesty until you notice how precisely that limited toolkit is being aimed.This is now his tenth century in all forms of T20 cricket, level with Virat Kohli for the most by an Indian batter, and his third T20I hundred, level with Samson, and behind only Rohit Sharma and Suryakumar Yadav in India's own list. The number worth sitting with isn't the 30 balls. It's how Abhishek has managed to keep his average above 30 while scoring at a strike rate of nearly 195.
Article Summary: Abhishek Sharma is the fastest T20I centurion ever produced by a Full Member nation. He averages 33.18 at a strike rate of 194.55 per 100 balls. He hits a six in T20Is every 7.58 balls, comfortably ahead of Finn Allen (8.47) and Travis Head (12.20) His strike rate in an innings' first ten balls is the joint-highest on the pitch.

World Cup goal is clear

NEW DELHI: Virat Kohli reached another major ODI milestone on Sunday, but the star batter made it clear that records and numbers have never been his main focus.Kohli became only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to complete 15,000 ODI runs. He also hit his record-extending 55th ODI century as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the first ODI.Kohli said his priority has always been to understand the situation and do what the team needs."My focus has never really been on these milestones, so to say. It's just understanding the situation along the course of just doing the job for the team, (the) achievements come along," Kohli told the broadcaster after the match.Kohli smashed nine sixes and 10 fours to remain unbeaten on 139 off 88 balls. India scored 300 for two in 41.4 overs while chasing West Indies' 295 for seven."Obviously, I feel very grateful and very blessed to be in this position for having played for so long. Just keeping my head down, working hard and thanking God for everything that I've been blessed with and the opportunities that I've got in my life to be where I am," Kohli said."We have a very blessed life and a blessed journey because so many people want to be here, but we get to be the lucky ones, so we better put our head down and just work hard every day of our lives," he added.Kohli said becoming more aggressive with the bat and playing at a higher gear has been a challenge for him at this stage of his career."… just the understanding of your game, firstly. Also, at the stage that I'm at, just keeping myself physically very fit because the game's more or less in the mind. I've never been a guy who practised a lot even when I was playing all three formats as you know," he replied to a query from former India coach Ravi Shastri."For me it's about about staying mentally fresh, staying in the present moment and just expressing myself really out there to play in a certain way, get used to this template more often.""I got a challenge at this stage of my career to kind of up the ante and play a gear or two higher and yeah, that was exciting for me to work on."He continued, "Again, it excites you when you have to unlock a new version at this stage of your career, which will eventually help any team that you play for, be it playing for India or in the IPL. It's really helped me a lot to play with a free mind and I think that's what's working for me."Kohli also spoke about the role of fitness in his batting and how it helps him visualise his game."I think to follow a free mind, you need a fit body so for me, it works the other way around. I stay physically fit and then I'm able to visualise the game in the way that I want to play, which allows me the best chance to go out there and execute in the way that I did tonight," he said.He also stressed the importance of remembering the journey that brought him to this stage."I think the only thing we need to do is just look back once and where we came from. That's something that we tend to forget when we are caught up with the hustle of the world and the positions we get into with so much attention and fame and so much love from the fans" he said."It can be very easy to forget where you came from. But just looking back at the journey from when you started as a child just makes you feel grateful."Kohli added, "I enjoy each and every minute that I'm out there playing for India because I understand that, as I said I could have been a possibility that I wouldn't be standing here. I wouldn't have played for India at all."The 37-year-old said playing only one format for India has also given him clarity about what he wants to achieve."We are a year away from the World Cup. I know what my goal is and it's pretty clear for me that whatever games we get, I just need to keep working on different aspects of the game, keep myself physically fit, challenge myself to be out there.""… run from boundary to boundary in the last 15 overs if I can, field in the inner ring, show intensity. If I keep ticking all those boxes, I've got some time left to play in this format as well.""So when I get an opportunity, I feel happy rather than feeling anxiety or pressure to make the most of it. I just want to express myself and play my game. As I said, I promised myself I'm going to play positively because I can.""I'm going to continue to play like that but not be reckless. There's a fine line, which as a professional, as an experienced player, I should have the ability to execute in this way without playing reckless shots and get the team through," he added.
Article Summary: Kohli became only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to complete 15,000 ODI runs. He also hit his record-extending 55th ODI century as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the first ODI. The 37-year-old said his priority has always been to understand the situation.

THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Virat Kohli brought up his record 55th ODI century with an emphatic six, marching past 15,000 runs in this format. India captain Shubman Gill also looked imperious, as he reached his 10th ODI hundred by unfurling his signature cuts and drives. Between them, India cantered to an 8-wicket win here at the Greenfield International Stadium in a chase that never once felt like a contest.A brilliant opening salvo from Rohit Sharma , whose 35-ball 32 laid the foundation for India’s pursuit, as the hosts eased past the 295-run target in 41.4 overs against a lacklustre West Indies bowling attack. India’s insouciance with the bat came after a clinical display from Kuldeep Yadav, his wrist-spin ripping through the West Indies middle-order with a four-wicket haul. This match was a lesson in class, distance and everything in between.Gill and Kohli put together a 151-run stand for the second wicket that had the Thiruvananthapuram crowd on its feet, and for a while it looked like the two of them would see the chase home between them. Cramps and fatigue got the better of Gill, as he eventually walked off, his 110 off 108 balls, with 13 fours and a six, a knock that had class written through it.Kohli, still chasing down whatever he considers “unfinished business” before the 2027 World Cup, was unbeaten on a scarcely believable 88-ball 139 in the end, his tenth ODI ton against the West Indies.West Indies didn’t have much to show for in the afternoon, but they did have Justin Greaves. Asked to bat first, the visitors leaned almost entirely on their opener, who cracked a maiden ODI hundred, 101 off 108 balls, to drag the visitors to 295/7. He put on 135 for the first wicket with John Campbell, who chipped in with a breezy 62 off 60, and that stand alone was worth the price of admission: West Indies’ first century opening partnership in ODIs in two years.Just when the West Indies looked like running away with the game, Kuldeep spun a web with figures of 10-1-40-4. It was a tour-de-force performance by India’s virtuoso chinaman bowler who was playing a different contest to the rest of his teammates.After a string of wide deliveries that left West Indies batter John Campbell visibly tetchy, Kuldeep dropped one full and straight at the stumps. On cue, Campbell got provoked and went for a mistimed sweep that was picked up by Prasidh Krishna at backward square-leg. Kuldeep then conned West Indies captain Shai Hope with drift, eliciting a leading edge that ballooned towards Ravindra Jadeja at cover.Kuldeep’s most telling blow was the manner in which he dismissed opener Justin Greaves, who was trapped lbw after missing a sweep against a ball on a length on leg stump. Greaves’ departure set jitters in the visitors’ dressing room, and on the next delivery, the Kanpur spinner bamboozled Jewel Andrew with a googly to prise his fourth scalp.Kuldeep’s timely blows meant the West Indies would lose their momentum in the middle overs, capping a redemption for the 31-year-old, who endured a tepid Sri Lanka Test series. Whatever Kuldeep lost in Sri Lanka, he’s found it again in Thiruvananthapuram.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli scores record 55th ODI century as India beat West Indies. Shubman Gill hits 110 off 108 balls, with 13 fours and a six. Rohit Sharma scores 32 as India reach 295-4 in 41.4 overs. Kuldeep Yadav takes four wicket haul for India.

Article Title: 'I was distraught': Virat Kohli reveals defeat that was 'too tough to swallow'
Article Text:

'I feel the same about the World Cup final'

India's recent ICC success may have brought an end to their long-standing trophy drought, but some World Cup defeats continue to remain difficult memories for Virat Kohli India won back-to-back T20 World Cup titles before adding the Champions Trophy, but the heartbreak of November 19, 2023 still remains fresh in the minds of ardent cricket followers. Rohit Sharma has spoken about that defeat on several occasions.For Kohli , though, the 2019 World Cup semifinal loss to New Zealand remains an even more painful experience.The semifinal in Manchester stretched across two days after persistent rain interrupted New Zealand's innings in the 47th over. The Black Caps returned the following day to finish on 239/8 before India fell 18 runs short in the chase.The match is particularly remembered for MS Dhoni's heartbreaking run-out by Martin Guptill in the 49th over.Bhuvneshwar Kumar, who took three wickets in the game, recently described the defeat as "heartbreaking". Kohli agreed with his former India team-mate, admitting that the loss left him distraught.“Playing Australia in the 2015 semifinal, you are very well aware of your strength and weaknesses and Australia is always difficult. We always knew that if it gets to a massive score, it will be tough, and that is what happened.They were phenomenal.“But 2019 was a jolt for us. 240... it rained out. Had we played that day, things would have been different. But next morning, fresh new ball attack. They got the best of the conditions and they put us under attack and they banked on the hesitation that we had.“That was too tough to swallow and process. I was distraught. After that I was totally gone mentally for a couple of months,” he told JioStar ahead of India’s first ODI against West Indies.Kohli viewed India's run to the 2023 World Cup final differently, describing the campaign as a "massive step forward" in terms of both talent and performance.More than the results, however, he remembered the atmosphere within the squad and the way the players responded to setbacks.“That whole World Cup was great, the environment was phenomenal. Within the team, you could see the camaraderie; everyone was happy playing for each other.“Even losing someone like Hardik early on, we never spoke about what would happen next although it was a big loss in terms of what he brings. But, Shami came and you know what he can do.“So, everyone had a feeling that it was our World Cup,” he added.India's campaign ultimately ended with a defeat to Australia in the final in Ahmedabad, another result that Kohli found difficult to process.He compared the feeling to the flashbacks he experienced after the 2016 IPL final, which continued until Royal Challengers Bengaluru won the IPL in 2025.“Before we won the IPL in 2025, I used to get flashbacks of the 2016 final. I feel the same about the World Cup final as well.“I was playing on 54 and had set myself up for a big hundred; like, if I got 140-150, we would be in a great position to win that game.“But as soon as I played on, it was very tough to process for many days. And you keep thinking about it.”Kohli has confirmed that the 2027 ICC tournament will be his last World Cup for India. That decision has given his next campaign an added significance.“For me, it’s the last World Cup I’m going to play for India. And that is my motivation,” he added.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli recalls India's World Cup semifinal defeat to New Zealand in 2023. India were bowled out for 240 after rain interrupted their innings in the 47th over. The Black Caps returned the following day to finish on 239/8 before India fell 18 runs short in the chase. Kohli has confirmed that the 2027 ICC tournament will be his last World Cup for India.

Virat Kohli is once again on the cusp of an ODI milestone that would add another remarkable chapter to his extraordinary career. The former India captain needs just 59 runs in the opening ODI against West Indies in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday to become only the second batter in men's ODI history to reach the 15,000-run mark, joining Sachin Tendulkar in an exclusive club.Kohli has accumulated 14,941 runs in 314 ODIs and 302 innings at an average of 58.59, with 54 centuries and 79 fifties. Tendulkar remains the format's leading run-scorer with 18,426 runs, meaning Kohli's next landmark will place him alongside the player whose ODI records have defined Indian cricket for decades.But the 15,000-run mark is only one of several records within Kohli's reach.If Kohli scores the required 59 runs against West Indies, he will reach 15,000 ODI runs in his 303rd innings. That would make him the fastest batter to the landmark by a considerable margin. Tendulkar reached 15,000 runs in his 377th ODI innings in 2007. Kohli would therefore get there 74 innings earlier than his illustrious predecessor.The landmark would also fit into a pattern that has followed Kohli throughout his ODI career. He became the fastest batter to 13,000 ODI runs when he reached the mark in 267 innings in 2023, breaking Tendulkar's previous record of 321 innings.There is another layer to the milestone given the opposition. Kohli has enjoyed remarkable success against West Indies, scoring 2,261 runs in 43 matches and 41 innings at an average of 66.50. He has nine centuries and 11 fifties against them.Thiruvananthapuram has also been a productive venue for the right-hander. He has scored 199 runs without being dismissed in two ODIs at the venue, including his sensational unbeaten 166 against Sri Lanka in January 2023.Kohli has another Tendulkar record in his sights, the most ODI runs scored in home conditions. Tendulkar amassed 6,976 ODI runs in India. Kohli currently has 6,867, leaving him 110 runs short of overtaking the former India opener.Kohli's home ODI numbers underline his consistency. He has scored those 6,867 runs in 130 matches and 127 innings, averaging 62.42, with 27 centuries and 36 fifties.Kohli's pursuit of Tendulkar's records extends beyond ODIs. The former India captain currently has 85 international centuries and remains on the path towards the 100-century landmark that Tendulkar was the first to reach.At home, Kohli has 41 international hundreds, with Tendulkar's record standing at 42. Two more centuries in India would take Kohli past his former teammate and India's batting icon in that particular category.Kohli is also closing in on Tendulkar's record for most List-A centuries. Kohli has 59 List-A hundreds, while Tendulkar finished his career with 60. Since List-A cricket includes ODIs as well as other recognised 50-over matches, Kohli needs two more hundreds to move clear of Tendulkar at the top of the Indian list.

Balhara’s second Asiad podium finish

From Jakarta silver to Aichi-Nagoya bronze

NEW DELHI: India’s Pincky Balhara secured her second Asian Games medal in kurash, clinching bronze in the women’s -78kg category after losing 0-5 to South Korea’s Sumin Mo in the semifinals at Aichi-Nagoya on Monday.The 27-year-old thus added another medal to her Asian Games collection, eight years after winning silver in the women’s -52kg category at the 2018 Jakarta Games, when kurash made its debut at the continental event.Balhara’s latest podium finish also marked India’s third medal in kurash at the Asian Games. The Indian had reached the semifinals with a 3-0 victory over South Korea’s Garam Lim in the quarterfinals.Balhara began her campaign in the quarterfinals against Lim, where she secured a convincing 3-0 victory to book her place in the last four. The Indian produced the decisive score through a ‘Chala’, a scoring move awarded when a competitor throws an opponent but does not demonstrate complete control over the action.Lim, meanwhile, failed to register a point during the contest, allowing Balhara to progress to the semifinals and put herself in contention for another Asian Games medal.However, the Indian could not overcome Mo in the semifinals. The South Korean secured a 5-0 win, ending Balhara’s hopes of reaching the final and leaving her with the bronze medal.Mo earned a ‘Yonbosh’ point during the contest, while Balhara was penalised with a ‘Dakki’. The Indian was unable to recover from the disadvantage as the South Korean controlled the bout to seal her place in the final.Balhara first made her mark at the Asian Games in 2018, when she won silver in the women’s -52kg category in Jakarta. Kurash was introduced to the Games programme that year, giving Indian athletes an opportunity to compete for medals in the Uzbek martial art.Her silver medal was among India's early successes in the discipline, and her latest podium finish underlines her continued presence in the sport at the highest continental level.The Indian contingent added another medal through Balhara’s performance on Monday, taking its overall tally at the Games to 39, comprising four gold, 17 silver and 18 bronze medals.
Article Summary: Pincky Balhara secures second Asian Games medal in kurash. Indian loses 0-5 to South Korea’s Sumin Mo in semifinals at Aichi-Nagoya. 27-year-old added another medal to her collection, eight years after Jakarta silver.

During the call, he asked Yashvir to speak to the federation and be ready to take his place in India's javelin squad for the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya."At that time, I was training and was at home. I was resting when I got a call from Neeraj bhai. He told me, ‘Brother, I’ve suffered an injury. Talk to them further so that your name can be considered in my place." Yashvir told TimesofIndia.com."After that, my name was included," he added.The Asian Games call-up came as a surprise to Yashvir, but his recent performances had put him in contention for a place in the squad. Yashvir had won a bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with a personal best of 85.41m. Chopra finished second in the same event.Yashvir's bronze came after a dramatic final throw. Before his last attempt, he spoke to Chopra and then told himself, "aaj to aar ya paar"."Before the competition, he motivated me a lot. We also spoke before my last throw," Yashvir said.He then produced his personal best of 85.41m to finish on the podium.With Chopra out of the Asian Games, Yashvir will join Rohit Yadav in India's men's javelin team. His 85.41m throw in Glasgow has given him confidence, but Yashvir knows he will face another big challenge in Aichi-Nagoya.After seeing his name in the Asian Games squad, Yashvir spoke to Chopra again. The Olympic medallist encouraged him to make the opportunity count.“He told me, ‘You did well at the Commonwealth Games. Now try to do well at the Asian Games too. Try to win a medal and give it your hundred percent”. Yashvir said.Yashvir believes his preparation is on the right track and is hoping to add another medal to his cabinet.“I’ve focused a lot on my technique. I’m physically fit as well. Now I just have to go there and perform. I dream of doing well,” he said.For Yashvir, the opportunity may have come unexpectedly, but he knows what he has to do when he takes the javelin in his hand again - give his best and fight for another medal in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: Yashvir Singh called by Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra. Chopra ruled out of Asian Games with ankle ligament injury. Yashvir had won bronze medal at Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. He will join Rohit Yadav in India's men's javelin team for 2026 Asian Games.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026 Day 8: Athletics leads India’s seven-medal haul, three boxers assure medals
Article Text:
Sarvesh Kushare, Parul Chaudhary and Tejaswin Shankar

Athletics produces five-medal haul

Anahat, Abhay win squash silver

Three boxers assure medals

Badminton suffers quarterfinal exits

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More action across disciplines

NEW DELHI: India enjoyed another productive day at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, adding seven medals on Sunday as athletics emerged as the biggest contributor with five podium finishes, while squash delivered two silver medals.The medal haul included silver medals for Ancy Sojan and Sarvesh Kushare, bronze medals for Parul Chaudhary, Tejaswin Shankar and Harita Bhadra, and two silver medals in squash through Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh.India's boxing campaign also received a major boost, with Parveen Hooda, Ankush Panghal and Narender Berwal all assuring themselves of medals by reaching the semifinals in their respective categories.There was disappointment in badminton, however, as PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda, Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand and Tanisha Crasto-Dhruv Kapila all bowed out in the quarterfinals of their individual events.Athletics provided India with its biggest haul of the day. Parul Chaudhary produced one of the standout performances , breaking her personal best and setting a new national record of 9:08.67 to win bronze in the women's 3000m steeplechase. It was Parul's second Asian Games steeplechase medal after she won silver in the same event at Hangzhou in 2022.Bahrain's Winfred Yavi won gold in 9:04.36, while Kazakhstan's Norah Jeruto Tanui took silver in 9:06.82. India's Ankita also set a personal best of 9:19.24 but finished fourth. Ancy Sojan came agonisingly close to gold in the women's long jump . Her 6.53m effort in the fifth round put her in front, but China's Huang Yingying produced a 6.55m jump with her final attempt to snatch the title by two centimetres.Shaili Singh was also denied a medal in the final round. Her 6.42m had put her third, but China's Mengyi Tan jumped 6.46m with her final attempt to move into bronze-medal position.In the men's high jump, Sarvesh Kushare also had to settle for silver after a closely fought contest. He cleared 2.25m on his second attempt, but Chinese Taipei's Chao Hsuan-Fu had already cleared the height on his first attempt. Tejaswin Shankar completed India's athletics medal haul with bronze in the decathlon . After two gruelling days, Tejaswin won the final event, the 1500m, in 4:33.09 and finished with 7,934 points. Japan's Yuma Maruyama won gold with 8,123 points, while China's Xinghua Chen took silver.Earlier, Harita Bhadra won bronze in the women's 200m , clocking 23.20 seconds to edge Japan's Ido Abigeirufuka by 0.01 seconds. Singapore's Shanti Pereira won gold in 22.78s and China's Chen Yujie took silver in 22.93s.India's wait for a squash singles gold at the Asian Games continued, but both Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh produced historic silver-medal finishes World No. 5 Sivasangari Subramaniam defeated 18-year-old Anahat 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in the women's singles final, while world No. 17 Ng Eain Yow beat Abhay 11-9, 11-5, 11-5 in the men's final.Malaysia therefore swept both singles gold medals.For Anahat, the silver was nevertheless a landmark achievement as she became the first Indian woman to reach an Asian Games squash singles final. The singles results also ended India's hopes of taking the direct qualification opportunity for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics through the Asian Games individual competition.While squash narrowly missed out on gold, Indian boxing delivered three guaranteed medals.Parveen Hooda defeated Uzbekistan's world championships silver medallist Navbakhor Khamidova 5-0 in the women's 65kg quarterfinal to reach the semifinals.It was Parveen's first bout of the Games after receiving a walkover in the previous round. She said she was beginning to regain confidence after returning from a suspension and moving up from 57kg to 65kg.Ankush Panghal also advanced with a dominant 5-0 win over Tajikistan's Nekruz Salimov in the men's 80kg quarterfinal. The Commonwealth Games gold medallist controlled the contest from the opening round and secured his Asian Games debut medal.Narender Berwal completed the trio of assured medals by stopping Thailand's Adthapong Saengtep in the men's 90+kg quarterfinal in less than two minutes. The Indian landed a barrage of heavy blows and forced three standing counts before the referee stopped the contest.The day ended in disappointment for Sachin Siwach, however, as the Commonwealth Games champion lost 0-5 to Japan's Shunsuke Kitamoto in the men's 60kg quarterfinal.Badminton provided one of India's biggest disappointments on Sunday.PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda, Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand and Tanisha Crasto-Dhruv Kapila all lost their respective quarterfinals, meaning India failed to win an individual badminton medal at the Games.Two-time Olympic medallist Sindhu, playing her third match in less than 24 hours, went down 21-11, 18-21, 10-21 to Tokyo Olympic champion Chen Yu Fei."It's a bit hurtful but I need to recover from this. It would have been good if I would have gone to the semifinals. Unfortunate but never mind, these things keep happening. It's important to get back stronger," Sindhu said.Unnati, 19, fought hard before losing 16-21, 21-14, 17-21 to three-time world champion Akane Yamaguchi.Treesa and Gayatri, who won a maiden World Championships bronze last month, lost 18-21, 9-21 to Malaysia's Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan. Tanisha and Dhruv also pushed world No. 1 Chinese pair Feng Yan Zhe and Huang Dongping before losing 14-21, 21-18, 18-21.India had won three badminton medals at Hangzhou, including men's doubles gold through Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, but none of the individual competitors could reach the semifinals this time.India also recorded important wins elsewhere. The women's hockey side beat Singapore 7-0, while the men's volleyball side defeated Vietnam 3-0.Indian archers advanced in all six team events contested, including the men's and women's compound teams, compound mixed team, recurve men's and women's teams, and recurve mixed team.In athletics, Mohammed Afsal qualified for the men's 800m final, while India's women's 4x100m relay quartet of Abinaya Rajarajan, Tamanna, Sneha Sathyanarayana and Sudeshna Shivankar topped its heat to reach the final.India also progressed in surfing and continued its campaign in shooting, while there were mixed results in fencing, sepaktakraw, kurash and equestrian.With seven medals added on Sunday and three more assured in boxing, Day 8 provided India with plenty of positives even as the medal tally remained short of the gold-medal gains needed to climb the standings.
Article Summary: Athletics provided India with its biggest haul of the day. Parul Chaudhary produced one of the standout performances. Parveen Hooda, Ankush Panghal and Narender Berwal all assured medals. PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda and Treesa Jolly- Gayatri Gopichand bowed out.

Article Title: India finish fifth in women’s 25m pistol team event; Esha Singh makes final, Manu Bhaker misses out

India slipped from second place to fifth in the women’s 25m pistol team event at the Asian Games 2026 on Monday, turning a promising start into another near-miss for the shooting contingent. Esha Singh , however, kept India's individual medal hopes alive by qualifying for the final.India had started the day strongly and were just one point behind leaders China after the precision stage. India have had both podium finishes and near-misses, with strong starts not always translating into medals.The disappointment will be sharper given India's record in the same event at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou. Esha won the individual bronze in the 25m pistol, while she, Bhaker and Rhythm Sangwan combined to win the team gold.Bhaker, meanwhile, had already made the women's 10m air pistol final at these Games but finished fifth. The men's 10m air pistol team finished fourth as well, with none of India's three shooters making the individual final.There have been podium finishes too.
